title: Normal forms
summary: Normal forms are constraints on functional dependencies. Second normal form bans partial dependencies of non-prime attributes. Third normal form allows a prime attribute on the right of a non-superkey; BCNF does not. BCNF implies 3NF.
intuition:
A functional dependency $X\to A$ says that any two legal tuples which agree on $X$ also agree on $A$. It is a constraint on the schema, not a coincidence in one table. $A$ is prime when $A$ belongs to some candidate key, and non-prime otherwise. The dependency is trivial when $A$ is already one of the attributes in $X$. Normal forms are restrictions on the nontrivial dependencies. They are not feature scaling: subtracting a minimum and dividing by a range is a different lesson, about numeric columns, and it does not put a relation into 3NF.

First normal form requires every attribute value to be atomic. A cell that holds a list of skills is not in 1NF; the multivalued attribute has to become its own relation before the later forms apply. Second normal form requires 1NF and forbids a partial dependency of a non-prime attribute: no non-prime $A$ is determined by a proper subset of a candidate key. If every candidate key is a single attribute, there is no proper subset that could cause this, and 2NF holds automatically. A composite key $\{\mathrm{sid},\mathrm{cid}\}$ with $\mathrm{sid}\to \mathrm{sname}$, and sname non-prime, is the violation.

Third normal form uses the definition that covers every nontrivial dependency, not only the transitive slogan. For every nontrivial $X\to A$, either $X$ is a superkey or $A$ is prime. Boyce-Codd normal form drops the second option: $X$ must be a superkey. Every dependency that satisfies BCNF therefore satisfies 3NF, so BCNF implies 3NF. The converse is false on a small pattern. Let the attributes be student, topic, and tutor, with $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}\to \mathrm{tutor}$ and $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$. Both $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}$ and $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{tutor}\}$ are candidate keys, so every attribute is prime. The dependency $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$ has a prime attribute determining another prime attribute, and topic depends on the key $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{tutor}\}$ through tutor. The left side is not a superkey and the right side is prime, so 3NF holds and BCNF does not.

definitions.body: $X\to A$ means that whenever two tuples agree on all attributes in $X$, they agree on $A$. The dependency is trivial when $A\in X$. The closure of $X$ is the set of attributes determined by $X$ through the declared dependencies.
An attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key. A non-prime attribute belongs to none. 2NF and the second clause of 3NF are statements about this distinction.
The relation is in 1NF, and no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key. A dependency of a prime attribute on a proper subset does not, by itself, violate 2NF.

3NF: for every nontrivial $X\to A$, $X$ is a superkey or $A$ is prime. BCNF: for every nontrivial $X\to A$, $X$ is a superkey. BCNF implies 3NF. A prime attribute determined by a non-superkey is the gap between them.

formulas.name: Third normal form
formulas.note: This is the definition to test. It is not $(x-\min)/(\max-\min)$.

formulas.name: Boyce-Codd normal form
formulas.note: Stricter than 3NF. The prime-attribute exception is gone, so BCNF implies 3NF.

properties: 1NF: every attribute value is atomic. A list stored in one cell is not in 1NF.
2NF: 1NF, and no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key. Single-attribute candidate keys cannot violate 2NF.
3NF: for every nontrivial $X\to A$, $X$ is a superkey or $A$ is prime.
BCNF: for every nontrivial $X\to A$, $X$ is a superkey. BCNF implies 3NF. The converse fails when a prime attribute determines another prime attribute and the determinant is not a superkey.
Rescaling a number, by a minimum and a maximum or by a mean and a standard deviation, is feature scaling. It is not a normal form.

examples.title: A partial dependency
examples.prompt: Enroll(sid, cid, sname, grade) has only the nontrivial dependencies $\mathrm{sid}\to \mathrm{sname}$ and $\{\mathrm{sid},\mathrm{cid}\}\to \mathrm{grade}$. Which normal form fails?
steps: The closure of $\{\mathrm{sid},\mathrm{cid}\}$ contains sname, by the first dependency, and grade, by the second, so it contains every attribute. The closure of sid is $\{\mathrm{sid},\mathrm{sname}\}$, missing cid and grade. The closure of cid is $\{\mathrm{cid}\}$. The only candidate key is $\{\mathrm{sid},\mathrm{cid}\}$.
sname is not in that key, so sname is non-prime. sid is a proper subset of the key and sid determines sname. That is a partial dependency of a non-prime attribute.

The cells are atomic, so 1NF holds. 2NF does not. A relation that is not in 2NF is not in 3NF or BCNF either. Splitting into Student(sid, sname) and Mark(sid, cid, grade) gives each dependency a key on its left.
examples.answer: The only candidate key is $\{\mathrm{sid},\mathrm{cid}\}$. The dependency $\mathrm{sid}\to \mathrm{sname}$ violates 2NF. This is a partial dependency, not a scaling of sname.

examples.title: In 3NF, and not in BCNF
examples.prompt: Teaches(student, topic, tutor) has $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}\to \mathrm{tutor}$ and $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$. Test 3NF and BCNF from the closures.
steps: The closure of tutor is $\{\mathrm{tutor},\mathrm{topic}\}$. Student is missing, so tutor is not a superkey. The closure of $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}$ is all three attributes, and neither attribute alone determines the others, so that pair is a candidate key.

The closure of $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{tutor}\}$ is also all three, because tutor determines topic, and neither student nor tutor alone is a key. So $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{tutor}\}$ is a second candidate key. Every attribute sits in some candidate key, and every attribute is prime.

The nontrivial dependency $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$ has a left side that is not a superkey, so BCNF fails. The right side topic is prime, so the 3NF exception applies and 3NF holds. Topic depends on the candidate key $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{tutor}\}$ through the prime attribute tutor. There is no non-prime attribute, so the 2NF ban has nothing to reject.
examples.answer: The relation is in 3NF and not in BCNF. tutor is not a superkey, topic is prime, and both $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}$ and $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{tutor}\}$ are candidate keys. BCNF would have required tutor to be a superkey.

traps: Using $(x-\min)/(\max-\min)$ as 3NF. That is min-max feature scaling. 3NF is a condition on functional dependencies.
Thinking 3NF implies BCNF. The tutor dependency is the counterexample: the right side is prime, the left side is not a superkey, and 3NF allows what BCNF forbids.
Calling tutor $\to$ topic a 2NF violation. 2NF restricts non-prime attributes, and in that relation every attribute is prime.
Testing a key on one table of rows. A candidate key is read off the closures of the declared dependencies. A column that happens to be unique today may not be a key.

questions.stem: Enroll(sid, cid, sname, grade) has candidate key $\{\mathrm{sid},\mathrm{cid}\}$ and the dependency $\mathrm{sid}\to \mathrm{sname}$, with sname in no candidate key. The relation
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**.

sname is non-prime, and sid is a proper subset of the only candidate key, so sid $\to$ sname is a partial dependency. That violates 2NF. The attributes are atomic, so this is not a 1NF failure. A relation that fails 2NF is not in BCNF. Option D is feature scaling, which does not mention a key.
options: violates 2NF because of a partial dependency
is an instance of min-max scaling

questions.stem: Teaches(student, topic, tutor) has $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}\to \mathrm{tutor}$ and $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$. The relation
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**.

The candidate keys are $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}$ and $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{tutor}\}$, so topic is prime and tutor is not a superkey. 3NF allows $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$ because the right side is prime. BCNF does not, because the left side must be a superkey. Option C would require a non-prime attribute, and there is none.
options: is in 3NF and not in BCNF
violates 2NF, because a non-prime attribute depends on part of a key

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

1NF is atomic attribute values. The 3NF test is exactly the superkey-or-prime condition, and the BCNF test keeps only the superkey half. Option D reverses the implication. Every BCNF dependency already satisfies 3NF, so BCNF implies 3NF; Teaches shows a relation that is in 3NF and not in BCNF, so 3NF does not imply BCNF.
options: 1NF requires every attribute value to be atomic.
3NF says that for every nontrivial $X\to A$, $X$ is a superkey or $A$ is prime.
BCNF says that for every nontrivial $X\to A$, $X$ is a superkey.

questions.stem: For Teaches(student, topic, tutor) with $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}\to \mathrm{tutor}$ and $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$, which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and D**.

Starting from tutor and applying $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$ produces $\{\mathrm{tutor},\mathrm{topic}\}$, not the student. Adding student to tutor produces topic as well, and the set is minimal, so $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{tutor}\}$ is a candidate key. Option C is false: tutor's closure misses student, so tutor is not a superkey and the dependency is exactly the BCNF violation. All three attributes are prime, which is why 3NF still holds.
options: $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$ has a superkey on the left, so it satisfies BCNF.
Every attribute is prime, which is why $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$ can satisfy 3NF while failing BCNF.

questions.stem: Using the dependencies $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}\to \mathrm{tutor}$ and $\mathrm{tutor}\to \mathrm{topic}$, how many attributes are in the closure of $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic}\}$?
questions.solution:
The answer is **3**.

The set already contains student and topic. The first dependency adds tutor. No fourth attribute exists. The closure is $\{\mathrm{student},\mathrm{topic},\mathrm{tutor}\}$, which has size $3$, and that is why the pair is a superkey.
